turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. What has you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this knee, doctor, the right one. Going down the stairs is a holy show, and then of a night it starts up on me again.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the stairs, in your own time.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): There's fourteen steps down to the hall, and the third from the bottom is the killer. I go down sideways, holding the rail like an old crab. Coming up isn't nearly as bad, which is odd.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has it been going on?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Five weeks. Well, no, I'm wrong — we had the communion early in the summer and I was grand then, so it's eight weeks. Definitely eight weeks.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And what is it like at night?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I get to bed grand enough, and then around two, maybe half two, it aches deep in the joint. The pillow between the knees was a waste of money, it goes flat. I end up sitting on the edge of the bed until it eases.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it swell, or lock, or give way under you?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It puffs up a small bit by the evening, over the kneecap. It doesn't lock, thank God. And it hasn't given way on me. I was worried after Josie next door went down in the supermarket, but that's her, not me.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any heat in the joint, or a fever with it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. And it's not hot if I put my hand on it. Just sore, and a bit puffy, as I said.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Where exactly do you feel the pain?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): On the inside of the right knee, and under the kneecap on the way down the steps. If I sit too long at mass it stiffens up, and the first few steps after are desperate.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been doing for it yourself?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): The gel from the chemist, diclofenac, the one percent. I rub a finger's worth into the right knee twice a day — actually, no, it's three times a day, morning, after the dinner, and before bed.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tablets along with the gel?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol by mouth, two of the five hundred milligram ones, most mornings. And now and again the diclofenac tablets, by mouth as well. I thought they were the twenty-five milligram, but I looked at the box this morning — they're fifty milligram.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often would you take the diclofenac tablet?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not every day. Maybe two evenings in the week, if the stairs have been bad. I never swallow two of them together. My sister takes hers every day for her back, but I'm not doing that.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any stomach trouble from them at all?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No stomach problems at all. I was careful about that, because my mother had an ulcer from tablets years back, and I didn't want the same.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. What else are you taking, prescribed or from the chemist?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure tablet, amlodipine, for the high blood pressure I've had for years. It was five milligrams for ages and then they put it up — no, sorry, it's ten milligrams now, by mouth, every morning.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I do miss it the odd morning, if I'm rushing to the half eight mass. Not often. Most days it goes down me.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the plan is every morning, but you're not dead sure it happens every single day.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the truth of it, yes.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else sitting in the press?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Gaviscon. A spoonful by mouth when I need it, usually in the evening.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn, is it?

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, yes. I said no stomach problems and I meant no pain in the stomach itself, but I do get heartburn of an evening, the last few weeks. If I take the diclofenac tablet and lie down on the couch for the news, it burns up behind the breastbone. A spoon of Gaviscon settles it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can you put any date on when that heartburn started?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I couldn't tell you. It crept up on me. Not years, just lately, and I can't pin the day at all.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting, black stools, or food sticking on the way down?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): None of that. No vomiting, the bowels are grand, no black stools, and nothing sticking.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. No allergies that I know of.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can I ask about your weight? It matters for a knee.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I know, I know. I'm after putting on a bit since I stopped the bowling. Too many biscuits with the tea, if I'm honest, and no one in the house to give out to me.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): The note from the nurse this morning has you at ninety-one point five kilograms.

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Those scales are miles out. I weighed myself at home yesterday, eighty-six — no, eighty-seven kilograms, in my socks, before the breakfast. I'd swear to the eighty-seven.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): So it's ninety-one point five on our note and eighty-seven on yours, and we won't settle which is right today.

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Put the eighty-seven down as the true one. I still had the coat on for your one, I'd say. Theirs always reads high. Still and all, eighty-seven is what my own scales said.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep both figures. How are you managing around the house and out of it?

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I live on my own since Paddy died, three years now. I was a primary teacher, retired ten years. I walk to mass most mornings, only about ten minutes and flat, though the hill home is another story. I gave up the bowling in the spring.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look at the knee now, if you're agreeable.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Fire ahead. It's the right one. The left never bothered me.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tender along the medial joint line of the right knee. There's a small effusion, nothing dramatic, and crepitus when I bend it. It straightens out fully, and there's no redness.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the exact spot, yes, when you press there. I got the same catch coming off the path outside the credit union last week.

[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, this sounds like osteoarthritis of the right knee, wear and tear. I'm not calling it certain — it's my working impression from the story and from that examination.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had the two knees done, so I was half waiting for it. She was eighty-two for the second one. I'm seventy-four in November, so I've a bit to go yet, please God.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you ever have an operation yourself, on the knee or anywhere else?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Cataracts, the both eyes — the left one three years ago, and the right the year before that. Nothing ever on the knee. No scope, no surgery there at all.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): For this knee, two roads are worth a chat. Physiotherapy, to build the muscle above the knee, or a steroid injection into the joint. I don't want to decide that for you today.

[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Would the injection be done here in the treatment room? Josie had one and she was flying for months, though she also said the first week was worse, so I don't know which part to believe. And is the physio the place down on the Mall?

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Either one is reasonable. Physio if you'd rather avoid a needle, the injection if the night pain is what you want eased sooner. We might do one, we might do the other. Nothing is booked.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I think about it, so? I want to ask my daughter. She'll say I'm being dramatic, but she doesn't have my stairs.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): You think on it. Nothing goes ahead until you say the word.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I picked the physio, how many times would I be trailing over there?
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Usually a short block of sessions, but we won't book it unless you want it. Same story for the injection — only if you decide you want it.

[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, keep the gel three times a day, that's fine. Go easy on the diclofenac tablets with that heartburn — take one with food if you take it, and don't lie down straight after.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll do that. I'll leave the Gaviscon by the couch so I don't have to go hunting in the press.

[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Easing even a small bit of weight off the knee would help, whichever number we believe. No crash diets. A bit more of the flat walking, and on the stairs try leading with the good leg on the way down.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Down with the good leg. I'll try it. I already hold the rail, ever since Mrs Kearney fell, and I'm not proud about it.
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in six weeks. We'll make the decision then, physio or the injection, once you've had time to think.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Should I be writing down the nights it wakes me?
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you like, a simple note of which nights it wakes you. It's not essential.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): What about an x-ray? They x-ray Josie every time she sneezes, near enough.
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might x-ray the knee if it's not settling by then, or if we head towards an injection. I'm not ordering one today.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand so. And the amlodipine — I stay on the ten milligrams?
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, stay on the ten milligram amlodipine every morning, and try not to skip it on the mass days. That one is doing a different job to the knee tablets.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): I will. And just so the file is right, the diclofenac tablet is the fifty, not the old twenty-five. I don't want the wrong strength written in.
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fifty milligram diclofenac, now and again, with food. The gel as you are already using it. Paracetamol in the mornings is fine alongside the both of them.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): Perfect. I'll go out the long way and skip the stairs. You've been very decent about it, doctor.
[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Mind yourself on the way out, and I'll see you in six weeks.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, please God. I'll have picked one or the other by then, or I'll have talked myself out of the pair of them, knowing me.

features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
